stimulus.text:
The British print shows four Loyalists hanged from a tree branch, with the words “Recommended to Congress by Lord S—” written above them. Below, three Native figures attack Loyalists: one holds a rope and says “I have them all in a String,” one holds a knife and says “I'll scalp him,” and one raises a tomahawk and says “I'll tomahawk the Dog.” A kneeling Loyalist cries, “O Cruel Fate! is this the Return for Our Loyalty.” The title reads “The Savages let loose, OR The Cruel FATE of the LOYALISTS,” with the captions “Is this a Peace, when Loyalists must bleed?” and “It is a Bloody Piece of work indeed.”
— The Savages Let Loose, London, 1783 (sold by W. Humphrey, 227 Strand)

stem: The print's complaint — “Is this a Peace, when Loyalists must bleed?” — refers most directly to the fact that the Treaty of Paris

options.text: Gave Canada to the United States as punishment for loyalty
options.misconception: Canada stayed British; the treaty gave the United States land to the Mississippi, not Canada.

options.text: Left Loyalists to states that seized their property and drove them away
Freed every enslaved person who had joined the British
options.misconception: The treaty freed no one; it said nothing about enslaved people, and many who had fled with the British were left to fend for themselves.

options.text: Forced Britain to pay the Loyalists for everything they had lost
options.misconception: Britain paid no such compensation; the treaty only asked Congress to recommend that states restore confiscated property.

rationales.B: The treaty recognized independence and set borders but left Loyalists to the states. Background: Congress could only recommend restitution, and many Loyalists had already fled to Canada, Britain, or the Caribbean.
rationales.A: Canada never changed hands; the treaty's border ran to the Mississippi, and Canada stayed British.
rationales.C: The treaty says nothing about enslaved people; freedom for those who joined Britain was never written into the peace.
rationales.D: No payment was required; the treaty asked Congress to recommend restoration, and the states largely refused.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the peace settled. Background: independence and borders — not the Loyalists.
2. Ask who decided their fate. Background: the states, which had seized Loyalist land and driven many away.
3. Ask what Congress could do. Background: it could only recommend restitution, which the states were free to refuse.
Remember: a treaty that is silent on a group has still decided its fate — ask who is left out of the terms.
